chief_complaint: binge eating followed by self-induced vomiting, normal weight
hpi_details: A 65-year-old male presents to the clinic with binge eating followed by self-induced vomiting, normal weight. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks his secret binge eating is just a shameful loss of willpower brought on by retirement stress, and that throwing up is the only practical way to keep from gaining weight.
concerns: He is terrified that his family will discover his secret vomiting routine and lose all respect for him.
expectations: He hopes to be prescribed an appetite suppressant pill to stop the uncontrollable cravings before they start.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Bulimia Nervosa is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Bulimia Nervosa: Fluoxetine (Prozac) 60mg, CBT, monitor electrolytes, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

must_ask.say: Can you describe what happens during an eating binge — how much you eat and how often it happens?
Do you make yourself vomit, use laxatives, or exercise excessively afterward?
How do you feel about your weight and body shape?
Have you noticed dental problems, throat irritation, or an irregular heartbeat?
Do you feel a loss of control during binges, and how much shame or secrecy is involved?

history.answer: I have been having episodes where I eat massive amounts of food and then force myself to vomit right after.
It began about three months ago and has been gradually getting worse, now happening almost every day.
I usually make myself vomit within twenty to thirty minutes after a binge, once or twice daily.
It is just whatever food I recently ate along with some stomach fluid, with no blood, bile, or foul odor.
No, I never wake up nauseated or vomit on an empty stomach, and it does not shoot out forcefully.
I feel heavily bloated and stuffed before vomiting, but I do not have true abdominal pain, and throwing up relieves that fullness.
My bowel movements have been normal and I can pass gas easily, without any constipation or diarrhea.
No fever or chills at all, and no one else around me has been sick.
No headache, stiff neck, dizziness, vision disturbances, or confusion.
No, I have not had any falls or hits to the head.
I can drink liquids without trouble, but my mouth feels somewhat dry and I have noticed my urine is a bit darker.
No excessive thirst or frequent urination, and I do not have diabetes.
No chest pain, racing heartbeat, or difficulty catching my breath.
history.topic: Chest pain and shortness of breath

history.answer: I have not started any new prescription drugs, and I do not use cannabis or other recreational drugs.
My weight has remained steady around seventy kilograms, but I am terrified of gaining even a single pound.
Yes, I stick my fingers down my throat over the toilet until I bring everything back up.
I consume very large amounts of bread, snacks, and sweets in under an hour, usually alone late at night.
I feel like I completely lose control and cannot stop eating, and I secretly hide the wrappers out of shame.
I'm terrified my wife will find out what I've been doing in the bathroom and look at me with complete disgust.
I have been feeling generalized fatigue and low energy lately, and my throat often feels raw from the vomiting.
No, I have not used any laxatives, water pills, enemas, or diet pills to get rid of food.
I feel guilty and distressed about doing this, but I have no thoughts of harming myself or wanting to die.
I think I've just lost my self-discipline with all the stress lately, and making myself throw up seemed like the only way to keep from getting fat.
I'm terrified my wife will find out what I've been doing in the bathroom and look at me with complete disgust.
I was hoping you could give me a strong prescription appetite suppressant so I don't get those overwhelming urges to gorge myself.
I have no past medical problems and have always been generally healthy.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been hospitalized.
I do not take any regular prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or vitamins.
I do not have any known allergies to medicines or foods.
I have never smoked in my life.
I only drink socially, having a beer once or twice a month at most.
I am a retired accountant living at home with my wife, though I have kept all of this hidden from her.
There is no family history of eating disorders, depression, or other mental health conditions.

exam.finding: Alert, well-nourished older male of normal body habitus, appearing slightly fatigued but in no acute distress.
Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, heart rate 74 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, temperature 36.6 C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
No significant orthostatic drop; standing blood pressure 114/74 mmHg with a pulse of 78 beats per minute.
Mild pharyngeal erythema and subtle dental enamel wear on lingual surfaces; bilateral parotid glands mildly prominent but non-tender; oral mucosa slightly dry.
Regular rate and rhythm; normal S1 and S2 with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally with normal respiratory excursion and no adventitious sounds.
Flat and symmetric abdomen with no surgical scars, caput medusae, or visible peristalsis.
Normoactive bowel sounds heard in all four quadrants with no abdominal bruits.
Abdomen is soft and non-tender throughout with no guarding, rigidity, or palpable organomegaly.
Normal skin turgor, brisk capillary refill under two seconds, and faint callusing on the dorsal aspect of the right index and middle knuckles.
Neck is supple with full range of motion; negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
Alert and fully oriented to person, place, and time with coherent thought process and no acute cognitive deficits.
